title: Fitting a flat panel radiator in a new position
subtitle: Drain the heating system, run new pipework to a new wall position, hang the radiator on new brackets, and refill and balance the system
excerpt: How to move a flat panel radiator to a new wall position. Covers draining the circuit, capping the old pipework, running new 15 mm copper pipe to the new location, fitting wall brackets, hanging the radiator, connecting valves, and refilling.
sourceNotes: Collins Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). UK trade heating and plumbing practice. CIBSE guide to central heating commissioning (open access).

glossaryTerms.definition: The manually adjustable or thermostatic valve on the flow (supply) side of a radiator that controls the water flow through it. A thermostatic radiator valve (TRV) adjusts flow according to room temperature. The return side has a lockshield valve, which is a non-user-adjustable valve that sets the circuit balance.

The flow-control valve on the return side of a radiator, fitted with a plastic cap to prevent casual adjustment. It is set by the heating engineer during commissioning to balance the flow across the circuit. When a radiator is moved, the lockshield valve setting is re-established by opening it fully and then closing by the number of turns specified for that circuit.

The small square-head or slotted valve at the top corner of a radiator that allows trapped air to be released from the circuit. After any pipework work or system refill, all radiators should be bled in order, starting at the radiator furthest from the boiler.

content.text: Moving a radiator to a new position means capping the existing pipework and running new 15 mm pipes to the new location. The

Switch off the boiler. Connect a hose to the drain-off cock at the lowest point of the circuit and run it to a drain. Open the drain-off cock and open the
on the upstairs radiators to allow air in and speed draining. Allow the circuit to drain fully before cutting any pipes.
Cap the old pipework and run new pipes

Cut the flow and return pipes at the old radiator position and cap them with end-stop fittings soldered in place. Run the new 15 mm flow and return pipes to the new radiator position. Clean each pipe end and fitting with emery cloth and apply flux before soldering. Use lead-free solder and a MAPP gas torch. Allow all joints to cool fully before applying pressure.
Fit the wall brackets and hang the radiator

Mark the bracket positions on the wall using the spirit level. The top of a standard panel radiator typically sits 150 to 200 mm below the windowsill and the bottom sits about 100 to 150 mm above the floor. Fix the brackets into studs or masonry anchors. Hang the radiator and check it is level.

Connect the radiator valve on the flow side and the lockshield valve on the return. Wrap male threads with PTFE tape. Refill the system through the feed-and-expansion tank or the filling loop, bleeding radiators as the water rises. Check all new joints for leaks while the system is cold, then repeat once the system is up to operating temperature. Set the boiler pressure to 1.0 to 1.5 bar.

attrs.symptom: New soldered joint weeps water after refilling
attrs.cause: Flux residue was not cleaned from the joint before soldering, the pipe end was not fully clean, or insufficient solder was applied.
attrs.fix: Drain the circuit, cut out the leaking fitting, and re-solder with freshly cleaned pipe and new flux. Clean flux residue from completed joints with damp cloth.

attrs.symptom: New radiator does not heat up after refilling
attrs.cause: Air is trapped in the radiator, or the lockshield valve was not reopened after fitting.
attrs.fix: Bleed the radiator with a bleed key until water runs out of the bleed valve. Check the lockshield valve is open.
